paras: The Nettleton railroad laborers' expulsion was the driving off of Black construction workers from a railroad line near Nettleton, Craighead County, Arkansas, in mid-August 1882 by armed men disguised as Ku Klux. The contractors and the railroad's president appealed to Governor T. J. Churchill, who ordered the county sheriff to protect the workers, and within a week the men were reported back at work. Papers across the country carried the story as a revival of the Ku Klux and a clash between white and Black laborers.

According to a Little Rock dispatch of August 17, trouble had existed for some time between white and colored laborers on the Memphis and Kansas City railroad in Craighead County. The Black workers were employed by the contractors Bethune, Smith & Co., whose name other papers printed as "Bethane," "Betheuse" or "Bethure." A Chicago Journal special from Little Rock said the whites objected to the employment of Black laborers, and a news note in the Evening Critic described "much opposition among the white laborers" on the line.

On August 16, by the account of the August 17 dispatch, the contractors telegraphed the company's attorney, Newman Erb, from Nettleton Station that "parties under the guise of kuklux" had forced their Black help to leave "under penalty of death." Their telegram added that they could not do their work unless protected and asked Erb to induce the governor to aid them. While Erb was meeting Churchill, a second telegram arrived from the railroad's president, G. H. Nettleton, reporting that armed men had made the laborers quit under threat of killing them and asking that the "negro force" be kept at work.

Other accounts described the attackers as masked men or as "bands of white men disguised as Ku-Klux" who visited the laborers and warned them to leave. Some summaries attributed the expulsion directly to the white laborers on the line. The reports name none of the workers and give no count of either side.

On August 17 Churchill telegraphed Sheriff Wm. T. Love at Jonesboro, three miles from Nettleton, to investigate the matter and protect the workmen, an order one paper rendered as protection "at all hazards." The Journal's special the next day reported great excitement, said the Black workers were "greatly alarmed, fearing assassination," and said the sheriff would arrest all parties suspected of "kukluxing" them. On August 22 the Memphis Appeal reported that the laborers had resumed work, the sheriff having taken the matter in hand and afforded them protection. No report of arrests, indictments or trials appears in the coverage.

The story reached the white press through two channels: the Little Rock dispatch quoting the employers' and governor's telegrams, and the Chicago Journal's special from the scene. The New-York Tribune headlined it "KU KLUX IN ARKANSAS," the Omaha Bee "Kluklux Revived," and the Rock Island Argus "LABOR RIOT." The Memphis Appeal, closest to the scene, called it a "LABORERS' WAR" between white and colored men and later referred to the attackers as "a gang of roughs."

Shorter versions ran in news-summary columns from Sacramento and Salt Lake City to Savannah, Knoxville and Dallas between August 18 and 24, under headlines such as "Negroes Intimidated by a White Mob" and "Anti-Negro Laborers." Most of these printed the employers' telegrams without comment, and their concern, like the railroad president's, was that the work force be kept on the job.

A Little Rock wire of August 18 dated the contractors' telegram August 17 rather than August 16, apparently restating the earlier dispatch. The line was called both the Memphis and Kansas City and the Springfield and Memphis railroad, the Memphis Appeal using both names in one report.

reader.title: Nettleton railroad laborers' expulsion
bases: Armed, disguised white men, described as or acting for white laborers who objected to Black labor, drove the contractors' Black railroad workers off the job under threat of death (A2, A4, A5, A9).

The contractors' telegram, a separate telegram from the railroad president and the governor's order (A5, A6), a separate Chicago Journal special from the scene (A3, A4, A10) and a Memphis follow-up (A18) agree that Black laborers were driven from work by threats.

accounts.label: Memphis follow-up
